title: Durga Comes Home
hookLine: a goddess shaped from river clay, welcomed home like a daughter, and sent back to the river
carry: the goddess comes home as a daughter
last: HUMBLER THAN A BLADE OF GRASS.

cards: Straw, bound tight with twine into the shape of a body. Then clay from the riverbank, pressed on in layers, smoothed by thumbs, left to dry, cracked, filled, smoothed again, in workshops along the river in Bengal.
Slowly a face appears: wide eyes, a calm mouth, many arms, a lion at her feet. Then paint, cloth, jewelry. By autumn she's ready, and families and neighborhoods carry her in.
Today, the Shakta stream at its most public, Durga Puja, and what happens to her at the end.

teach.b: The text behind Durga is the Devi Mahatmya, and it tells of her as a warrior: the gods pour their powers into her, she rides out on her lion, and defeats the buffalo demon none of them could.
That's the image in the clay, spear in hand. But in Bengal the festival tells a second story at the same time.

Durga is also Uma, daughter of the mountain king Himalaya and his wife Menaka. She's married to Shiva and lives far away on his mountain, and once a year she comes home to visit her parents, bringing her children.
So the festival feels like a homecoming. Bengali songs called agamani, songs of arrival, put words in the mother's mouth: is my Uma really coming? How thin has she gotten?
What has that husband of hers been feeding her? In Bengal, the fierce goddess and the daughter whose mother worries are one. On the last day, Vijaya, she has to go back.
Married women, in a custom called sindur khela, smear red vermilion on the goddess's face and on each other, the way you'd send a daughter off.

teach.h: THE CLAY GOES BACK TO THE RIVER
teach.b: Then the image, all that patient work, is carried to the river and lowered into the water, and the clay goes back where it came from.
It's the same move as Ganesha's clay: the divine invited into an image, honored, and given back. The goodbye is sad; afterward people visit, embrace, share sweets.
Behind us this week: Sambandar's song, Kannappa's eye, Tirumular's cows, the king and the merchant, Ramprasad's ledger, Chaitanya's street. Now a goddess who comes home, and goes.

how: At Durga Puja, Bengali Hindus install clay images of Durga in homes and neighborhood pavilions, worship her for the festival days, and on Vijaya Dashami immerse the image in a river or pond.

games.q: what does “bengal's shakta and vaishnava streams” mean?
o: two Bengali festivals that mark the start of the rains
Bengal's custom of building clay images for river spirits
Bengal's devotion to the Goddess and to Krishna, side by side

games.q: Durga comes home — tap the pairs.

s: in Bengal, Durga is only a warrior goddess
she's also Uma, a daughter coming home, whose mother worries about her.
at the end of the festival, the clay image is lowered into the water
the clay goes back to the river it came from.
the farewell day is followed by visits and sweets
the goodbye songs are sad, and the greeting afterward is happy.

games.q: the festival's last day. the clay image of Durga took long, patient work, and she's beautiful. what happens to her now?
o: she stays on display in the pavilion.
she's carried to the river and lowered into the water.
she's stored away until next year.
games.why: she's immersed. the daughter goes back to her husband's home, and the clay goes back to the river.

practice: On the in-breath, think of someone you love arriving, the door opening, their face, and let yourself be glad.
On the out-breath, think of letting them go again, the door closing, the car pulling away, and hold on to neither, just breathing the arriving and the leaving.
If you pray, you can hold that person before the Goddess, or before God, as they come and as they go.

wordCard.voice: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, Durga Puja: the warrior goddess welcomed home as Uma, the daughter, then given back to the river. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the goddess comes home as a daughter. A warrior, a daughter, and clay returned to the river. A week, kept.
